reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents a supposedly free MetaMask front-running or automated trading bot as an easy tutorial and directs users to a shortened download link with a password. It instructs users to disable antivirus and Windows SmartScreen during installation, creating a security-bypass mechanism tied to the promotion. The separate crypto-chart advertisements are visible but are not shown to be created or endorsed by the video creator.

citations.quote: PancakeSwap Front Run Contract Bot 2021 - EASY TUTORIAL
we are talking about a bot for MetaMask
Copy the address of the token we need and paste it into the bot
The trade will take place in BNB cryptocurrency
We specify its amount in certain windows and launch the bot

opening.argument: The presentation does not promise a guaranteed return. It describes a free Windows-only tool, tells viewers to stop it themselves if they choose, and closes with “Good luck,” which is compatible with an informal demonstration rather than a certainty of profit. The account says the bot waits for the price to rise, but that is a stated intended sequence, not a guarantee that the price will rise or that a viewer will make money. The available material therefore supports caution about an unverified trading tool, not a conclusion that the creator is deceptively soliciting funds.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats installation advice as proof of a scam mechanism, but the cited material does not establish that the creator requests credentials, deposits, or guaranteed returns. The description itself characterizes the files as clean, while the video describes a configurable tool rather than promising an outcome. A shortened link and password may warrant caution, but they do not by themselves prove deceptive solicitation.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: “Good luck” is merely a closing phrase, not a risk disclosure, and “completely free” does not make the trading activity safe. The description specifically tells users to disable antivirus and Windows SmartScreen, while the title identifies a front-run contract bot. Those details provide a concrete security-bypass concern even though the material does not prove a completed profit.

opening.argument: The content is most naturally read as an operational demonstration or technology tutorial. The title explicitly calls it an “EASY TUTORIAL,” and the narration explains how to copy a token address, set an amount, launch the tool, and observe what happens. It even says the user may stop the bot themselves. Showing a workflow and describing what appears on screen is not the same as certifying a financial product or promising viewers a return. The demonstration may be technically questionable, but the evidence supports an educational framing centered on tool operation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution infers promotion from the title and workflow, but those same details are consistent with a tutorial: the narrator explains configuration and demonstrates operation. The material does not say viewers will definitely profit, nor does the narration establish that the displayed transaction completed successfully. A download option can accompany educational software without converting every explanation into a scam.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not neutralize what is being taught. The title specifically calls it a “Front Run Contract Bot,” and the narration instructs the viewer through token selection, BNB amount configuration, and launch. The absence of a proven completed profit does not change that the video presents a money-making trading mechanism for use.

The trade will take place in BNB cryptocurrency
We specify its amount in certain windows and launch the bot
now it will wait for the price to rise and sell it for more than the purchase price

opening.argument: At most, this is a software-and-trading demonstration involving an ordinary tool and an exchange interface. The narration does not show the creator collecting money, requesting a wallet password or credentials, recruiting a downline, or guaranteeing a return. It describes entering a token address and an amount in BNB, then observing the bot and balance. The stated plan to sell above the purchase price is a trading objective, not proof that the objective was achieved. Without a demonstrated deposit to the creator or a guaranteed outcome, the supplied evidence does not establish a scam mechanism.

The narrated workflow concerns a token trade in BNB and a bot balance, not payment to the speaker. Even the claimed resale is described as something the bot will wait to do, so the evidence does not show a completed return or a guaranteed one.

The trading workflow itself connects user-supplied BNB and a promised resale objective; calling that ordinary commerce overlooks the unusually risky mechanism being promoted.
